chapters.title: Why Do the Wicked Live?
chapters.html:
Job 21

1Job answered and said:

Listen and Be Appalled

2Listen closely to my words,
and let this be the comfort you give me.

3Bear with me, and I will speak,
and after I have spoken, mock on.

4As for me, is my complaint against man?
Why should my spirit not be short?

5Look at me and be appalled,
and lay your hand over your mouth.

6When I remember it, I am dismayed,
and shuddering seizes my flesh.

The Prosperity of the Wicked

7Why do the wicked live,
grow old and become mighty in power?

8Their offspring are established in their presence,
and their descendants before their eyes.

9Their houses are safe from fear,
and no rod of God is on them.

10Their bull breeds and does not fail;
their cow calves and does not miscarry.

11They send out their little ones like a flock,
and their children dance.

12They sing to the tambourine and the lyre
and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.

13They spend their days in prosperity,
and in a moment they go down to Sheol.

14They say to God, "Depart from us!
We do not desire the knowledge of Your ways.

15What is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?
What profit do we get if we pray to Him?"

16Their prosperity is not in their own hand;
the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

17How often is the lamp of the wicked put out?
How often does their disaster come on them,
or does He deal out pains in His anger?

18How often are they like straw before the wind,
like chaff that the storm carries away?

19You say, "God stores up a man's iniquity for his children."
Let Him repay it to the man himself, so that he knows it.

20Let his own eyes see his ruin,
and let him drink of the wrath of the Almighty.

21For what does he care for his house after him,
when the number of his months is cut off?

One Dies, Another Dies

22Will anyone teach God knowledge,
when He judges those on high?

23One dies in his full strength,
wholly at ease and secure,

24his pails full of milk
and the marrow of his bones moist.

25Another dies in bitterness of soul,
never having tasted of good.

26They lie down alike in the dust,
and the worms cover them.

27I know your thoughts,
and the schemes with which you would wrong me.

28For you say, "Where is the house of the prince?
Where is the tent in which the wicked lived?"

29Have you not asked those who travel the roads,
and do you not accept their signs,

30that the evil man is spared in the day of disaster,
that he is led away in the day of wrath?

31Who declares his way to his face,
and who repays him for what he has done?

32When he is carried to the grave,
watch is kept over his tomb.

33The clods of the valley are sweet to him;
all mankind follows after him,
and those who went before him are without number.

34How then will you comfort me with empty breath?
Nothing is left of your answers but faithlessness.

Notes

  • v4 "Why should my spirit not be short?" — lo tiqtsar ruchi, the Hebrew for impatience. Job's complaint is against God, not man, and so his patience has run out.

  • v7 "Why do the wicked live?" — Job answers Zophar's teaching of 20:5, the exulting of the wicked is short; Why does the way of the wicked prosper? (Jeremiah 12:1; Psalm 73:3–12).

  • vv14–15 "Depart from us… What is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?" — the words of the wicked, quoted by Eliphaz in 22:17.

  • v16 "the counsel of the wicked is far from me" — Job distances himself from the wicked even while describing their success. Eliphaz repeats the line word for word in 22:18.

  • vv17–18 "How often…?" — Job's challenge to Bildad's the light of the wicked is put out (18:5): it does not happen often. Like chaff that the storm carries away is the picture of Psalm 1:4.

  • vv19–21 — the Hebrew moves to the singular, a man… his children: it is not justice if a man's sons pay for his sins after he is dead and cannot know it (Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–4).

  • v24 "his pails full of milk" — atinav, a word found only here; it may mean his body or loins, full of fat.

  • vv23–26 — the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked (Ecclesiastes 9:2–3).

  • v29 "those who travel the roads" — men who have seen the world, and can tell that the wicked are not punished as the friends say.

  • v34 "empty breath… faithlessness" — hevel and ma'al, the word for unfaithfulness to God (Leviticus 5:15; Joshua 7:1): the friends' answers are not only empty but false.

chapters.title: Eliphaz's Third Speech
chapters.html:
Job 22

1Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

Is Not Your Evil Great?

2Can a man be of use to God?
Surely the wise man is of use to himself.

3Is it any pleasure to the Almighty if you are in the right,
or gain to Him if you make your ways blameless?

4Is it for your fear of Him that He reproves you
and enters into judgment with you?

5Is not your evil great?
There is no end to your iniquities.

6For you took pledges from your brothers for nothing
and stripped the naked of their clothing.

7You gave no water to the weary to drink,
and you withheld bread from the hungry.

8The man with power, the land was his,
and the favored man lived in it.

9You sent widows away empty,
and the arms of the fatherless were crushed.

10Therefore snares are all around you,
and sudden terror overwhelms you,

11or darkness, so that you cannot see,
and a flood of water covers you.

What Does God Know?

12Is not God high in the heavens?
See the highest of the stars, how high they are!

13But you say, "What does God know?
Can He judge through the thick darkness?

14Thick clouds hide Him, so that He does not see,
and He walks on the circle of the heavens."

15Will you keep to the old way
that wicked men have trodden?

16They were snatched away before their time;
their foundation was poured away by a river.

17They said to God, "Depart from us,"
and, "What can the Almighty do to us?"

18Yet He filled their houses with good things;
the counsel of the wicked is far from me.

19The righteous see it and are glad;
the innocent laugh them to scorn:

20"Surely our adversaries are cut off,
and what they left the fire has consumed."

Return to the Almighty

21Come to terms with Him, and be at peace;
by this, good will come to you.

22Receive instruction from His mouth,
and lay up His words in your heart.

23If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up;
if you remove injustice far from your tents,

24if you lay your gold in the dust,
and the gold of Ophir among the stones of the stream bed,

25then the Almighty will be your gold
and your silver in heaps.

26For then you will delight yourself in the Almighty
and lift up your face to God.

27You will pray to Him, and He will hear you,
and you will pay your vows.

28You will decide on a matter, and it will be established for you,
and light will shine on your ways.

29When they are brought low, you will say, "Lift them up!"
and He will save the one whose eyes are lowered.

30He will deliver even one who is not innocent,
who will be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.

Notes

  • vv2–3 "Can a man be of use to God?" — Eliphaz's view: God gains nothing from a man's goodness, so He has no reason to test a righteous man. The prologue (1:8; 2:3) shows that God delights in Job.

  • v4 "Is it for your fear of Him?" — the irony is complete: the reader knows that it is precisely for his fear of God that Job is being tested.

  • v6 "pledges… for nothing" — taking a man's cloak as a pledge for a loan and keeping it overnight, which the law forbade (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–13). For nothing is chinnam again (1:9; 2:3; 9:17). Eliphaz invents these sins; Job answers each in chapters 29 and 31.

  • v8 "the man with power, the land was his" — the line seems to describe Job as the powerful man, the man of arm, who held the land for himself and his favorites.

  • vv13–14 "What does God know?" — Eliphaz puts in Job's mouth the words of the wicked (Psalm 73:11; Isaiah 29:15). The circle of the heavens is the vault over the earth (Isaiah 40:22; Proverbs 8:27).

  • v16 "poured away by a river" — the flood of Noah's day, or any sudden flood that washes away a house built on sand (Matthew 7:26–27).

  • v18 — Eliphaz repeats Job's words of 21:16 word for word, the counsel of the wicked is far from me, perhaps in mockery.

  • v24 "the gold of Ophir" — the finest gold, from a land in Arabia or East Africa (1 Kings 9:28; Psalm 45:9). Job is to throw away his treasure; the Almighty will be his gold.

  • v29 — the Hebrew is hard. Gevah, read here as lift up, may also mean pride: when they are brought low, you will say, "It was pride."

  • v30 "He will deliver even one who is not innocent… through the cleanness of your hands" — i-naqi, not innocent. Without knowing it, Eliphaz foretells his own case: in 42:7–9 God forgives the three friends through Job's prayer.

chapters.title: Oh That I Knew Where to Find Him
chapters.html:
Job 23

1Job answered and said:

I Would Lay My Case Before Him

2Even today my complaint is bitter;
my hand is heavy on my groaning.

3Oh that I knew where I might find Him,
that I might come even to His seat!

4I would lay my case before Him
and fill my mouth with arguments.

5I would know the words He would answer me
and understand what He would say to me.

6Would He contend with me in the greatness of His power?
No; He would surely pay attention to me.

7There an upright man could argue with Him,
and I would be delivered forever by my judge.

When He Has Tested Me

8But I go forward, and He is not there,
and backward, but I do not perceive Him;

9on the left, when He is at work, I do not catch sight of Him;
He turns to the right, and I do not see Him.

10Yet He knows the way that I take;
when He has tested me, I will come out as gold.

11My foot has held fast to His steps;
I have kept His way and not turned aside.

12I have not departed from the commandment of His lips;
I have treasured the words of His mouth more than my portion.

13But He is one, and who can turn Him back?
What His soul desires, that He does.

14For He will complete what He has decreed for me,
and many such things are with Him.

15Therefore I am dismayed at His presence;
when I consider, I am in dread of Him.

16God has made my heart faint;
the Almighty has dismayed me.

17Yet I am not silenced by the darkness,
nor by the thick darkness that covers my face.

Notes

  • v2 "my hand is heavy on my groaning" — the Greek and Syriac read His hand is heavy, God's hand on Job, as in 19:21. The Hebrew may mean that Job holds back his groaning with his own hand.

  • v3 "His seat" — tekhunato, His fixed place, His dwelling; Job longs to find God's court and plead there.

  • v7 "delivered forever by my judge" — Job no longer fears the trial he dreaded in 9:14–20; he is sure that a fair hearing would clear him.

  • vv8–9 forward, backward, left, right — qedem, achor, semol and yamin are also east, west, north and south, for a man who faces the sunrise. Job has searched the four quarters of the world.

  • v10 "when He has tested me, I will come out as gold" — gold refined by fire (Zechariah 13:9; 1 Peter 1:7). Job does not know that he is being tested (1:11–12), but he says it.

  • v12 "more than my portion" — me-chuqqi, more than my allotted food; the Greek reads in my bosom. Your words were found, and I ate them (Jeremiah 15:16); Man shall not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3).

  • v13 "He is one" — hu ve-echad, He is in one: one in mind, unchangeable; the same words as the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), but here a source of dread.

  • v17 "Yet I am not silenced by the darkness" — the Hebrew is hard; it may also be read I am undone because of the darkness. As read here, Job is still speaking in spite of it.

chapters.title: Why Are Times Not Kept?
chapters.html:
Job 24

The Poor of the Earth

1Why are times not kept by the Almighty,
and why do those who know Him not see His days?

2Some move boundary stones;
they seize flocks and pasture them.

3They drive away the donkey of the fatherless;
they take the widow's ox as a pledge.

4They push the needy off the road;
the poor of the earth all hide themselves.

5Like wild donkeys in the wilderness
they go out to their work, searching for food;
the desert gives bread for their children.

6They gather fodder in the field
and glean the vineyard of the wicked man.

7They spend the night naked, without clothing,
and have no covering in the cold.

8They are wet with the rain of the mountains
and cling to the rock for lack of shelter.

9There are those who snatch the fatherless child from the breast
and take a pledge from the poor.

10They go about naked, without clothing;
hungry, they carry the sheaves;

11among the olive rows they press out oil;
they tread the winepresses, and are thirsty.

12From the city the dying groan,
and the soul of the wounded cries for help;
yet God does not count it wrong.

Rebels Against the Light

13There are those who rebel against the light;
they do not know its ways,
and do not stay in its paths.

14The murderer rises before daylight
to kill the poor and needy,
and in the night he is like a thief.

15The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight,
saying, "No eye will see me,"
and he puts a cover over his face.

16In the dark they dig through houses;
by day they shut themselves in;
they do not know the light.

17For deep shadow is morning to all of them;
they are friends with the terrors of deep shadow.

Swift on the Waters

18They are swift on the face of the waters;
their portion is cursed in the land;
no one turns toward their vineyards.

19Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters;
so does Sheol those who have sinned.

20The womb forgets him; the worm feeds sweetly on him;
he is remembered no more,
and injustice is broken like a tree.

21He wrongs the barren woman who does not bear,
and does no good to the widow.

22Yet He drags off the mighty by His power;
they rise up, and no one is sure of life.

23He gives them security, and they are supported,
and His eyes are on their ways.

24They are lifted up a little while, and then they are gone;
they are brought low and gathered up like all others;
they are cut off like the heads of grain.

25If it is not so, who will prove me a liar
and make my words worth nothing?

Notes

  • v1 "Why are times not kept by the Almighty?" — times of judgment set aside for the wicked; His days are the days when He brings justice (Isaiah 2:12; Amos 5:18).

  • v2 "Some move boundary stones" — forbidden by the law, You shall not move your neighbor's landmark (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17; Proverbs 22:28).

  • vv2–12 — the sins Eliphaz charged Job with (22:6–9) are done every day by others, and God does not act.

  • v5 "Like wild donkeys in the wilderness" — the poor, driven from their land, live like wild animals foraging (30:3–8).

  • v11 "among the olive rows" — shurotam, their rows, the terraces or walls of the olive groves. The poor press oil and tread grapes for others and go thirsty themselves (Deuteronomy 25:4).

  • v12 "God does not count it wrong" — lo yasim tiflah, the word of 1:22, where Job did not charge God with wrong; now he says God does not charge the wicked.

  • vv13–17 rebels against the light — the murderer, the adulterer and the thief work in darkness; everyone who does wicked things hates the light (John 3:20).

  • vv18–24 — these verses describe the swift end of the wicked, as the friends do (18:5–21; 20:5–29), and sit oddly in Job's mouth. They may be Job quoting the friends' view, or they may belong to a speech of one of the friends, perhaps Zophar's missing third speech. The text is rendered as it stands.

  • v20 "the worm feeds sweetly on him" — metaqo rimmah, the worm finds him sweet; compare 21:33, where the clods of the valley are sweet to him.

  • v22 "no one is sure of life" — lo ya'amin ba-chayyin, he does not trust in life; the line may mean that even the mighty, when God drags them off, despair of living.

Rebels Against the Light
There are those who rebel against the light; they do not know its ways, and do not stay in its paths.
The murderer rises before daylight to kill the poor and needy, and in the night he is like a thief.
The eye of the adulterer also waits for the twilight, saying, "No eye will see me," and he puts a cover over his face.
In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in; they do not know the light.
For deep shadow is morning to all of them; they are friends with the terrors of deep shadow.
Swift on the Waters
They are swift on the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the land; no one turns toward their vineyards.
Drought and heat snatch away the snow waters; so does Sheol those who have sinned.
The womb forgets him; the worm feeds sweetly on him; he is remembered no more, and injustice is broken like a tree.
He wrongs the barren woman who does not bear, and does no good to the widow.
Yet He drags off the mighty by His power; they rise up, and no one is sure of life.
He gives them security, and they are supported, and His eyes are on their ways.
They are lifted up a little while, and then they are gone; they are brought low and gathered up like all others; they are cut off like the heads of grain.
